result:
There is a particular hour, somewhere between five and six in the morning, when the apartment is so quiet you can hear the refrigerator cycling. I stand at the counter in just a t-shirt, hair still tangled from sleep, and I do the thing with the coffee. Measure the grounds. Watch the water hit the filter and bloom. The first dark drip.

The kitchen tile is cold under my bare feet. Outside the window, the neighbor's streetlight hasn't gone out yet, and it pools yellow on the back of my hands while I pour. There is no one to serve. No one waiting. The coffee is for the version of me who will be tired by three, who will need the small ceremony of a second cup at four, who will talk to the plant on the windowsill because the silence has started to feel like a question.

I don't make it for the caffeine. I make it for the four minutes it takes, the four minutes where I am not yet the person I will be at seven, not yet answering emails, not yet performing competence. Just hands and heat and the smell of something going from green to dark to bitter to warm.

The streetlight finally clicks off. A car passes, slow, its headlights washing the kitchen in pale blue. I drink the first sip standing up, not yet sitting down, not yet beginning.

This is the part I keep. Not the coffee. The four minutes of it.
